chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the New York City Council Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection, asks everyone to silence their devices, and instructs that no one approach the dais before handing the floor to the chair.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and gives housekeeping instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to the New York City Council vote for the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please put all devices on silent and no one should approach the dais.

chapters.summary: Chair Harvey D. Epstein welcomes everyone to the Consumer and Worker Protection Committee vote on Proposed Intro 891-A, sponsored by Speaker Menon, relating to surveillance pricing. He identifies himself as chair of the committee.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein convenes vote on Intro 891-A on surveillance pricing

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Welcome to today's Consumer Worker Protection Committee vote on proposed intro 891A, sponsored by Speaker Menon, Relationships of Failure and Pricing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm Harvey Epstein, chair of the committee.

chapters.summary: Chair Epstein lists the colleagues joining him — Brewer, De La Rosa, Krishnan, Osei, Shulman, Aldebol, and Wilson — and confirms that the committee has quorum to proceed.
chapters.title: Epstein announces attending members and confirms quorum

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm joined by my colleagues, Brewer, De La Rosa, Krishnan, Osei, Shulman, Adabal, Wilson.

chapters.summary: Chair Epstein explains that New Yorkers expect shelf labels with the same price for every shopper, but notes that before the 1800s consumers had to haggle, letting merchants charge different amounts based on willingness to pay.
chapters.title: Epstein recounts the history of haggling and fixed prices

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So when New Yorkers go to the store, we generally expect that we can look at a tag or a shelf label to see how much an item costs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: These prices are typically not negotiable, and we expect them to be the same for every shopper, at least in the short term.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But shopping has not always been this way.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Before the 1800s, consumers largely had to haggle over a price of goods and services they wished to purchase.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This allowed merchants to charge different consumers different amounts for the same product, depending on the individual's willingness to pay.

chapters.summary: Chair Epstein describes how some viewed variable pricing as morally wrong, and how Macy's founder Roland H. Macy began putting price tags on goods in the 1870s, benefiting both consumers and shopkeepers by simplifying comparison, training, and accounting.
chapters.title: Epstein credits Macy's with pioneering price tags in the 1870s

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Even these economic realities are always a group of people who believe it was morally wrong to charge different prices for the same goods.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: One of those people was the founder of Macy's, Roland Hussie Macy's, began putting price tags.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It turned out these prices would benefit both consumers and shopkeepers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Consumers could easily compare shops while stores can make, train new employees, simplify accounting systems, and it really saved time for everyone from all the haggling.

chapters.summary: Chair Epstein explains that modern technology lets businesses use consumer personal data to offer different prices for the same goods and services, a practice known as surveillance pricing. He states that Intro 891 would prohibit businesses from engaging in it.
chapters.title: Epstein defines surveillance pricing and the purpose of Intro 891

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Today's technology has changed the system.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Businesses are able to use consumer personal data to offer different price options to different consumers with the same goods and services.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's a practice known as surveillance pricing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: To today's intro, 891, prohibit businesses from engaging in surveillance pricing.

chapters.summary: Chair Epstein congratulates the Speaker on the bill, calling it a major step toward transparency and consistency in pricing and discounts offered to consumers, before moving to the vote.
chapters.title: Epstein praises Speaker and bill's transparency goals

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I congratulate the speaker on the bill, which is a major step on transparency, consistency around pricing and discounts offered to consumers.

chapters.summary: Chair Epstein asks the committee clerk to call the roll call vote on Intro 891-A.
chapters.title: Epstein directs the clerk to call the roll

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I now ask the clerk to call the roll call.

chapters.summary: Committee Clerk Ben Jacobs identifies himself and announces that this is the roll call vote on Intro 891-A, beginning with Chair Epstein.
chapters.title: Clerk Ben Jacobs opens roll call vote on Intro 891-A

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection, Ben Jacobs, Committee Clerk.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: This is the roll call vote on Intro 891A.

chapters.summary: Chair Epstein votes yes, and Council Member Gale A. Brewer votes yes on Intro 891-A.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein and Council Member Brewer vote yes

chapters.summary: Council Member Brewer explains that she understands the state has passed a compatible bill awaiting the governor's signature, noting this was a concern of hers, and thanks the chair.
chapters.title: Brewer notes compatibility with pending state legislation

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes, it's my understanding, too, that the state is considering, has passed, the governor hopefully will sign, and that these bills are compatible.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That was a concern of mine.

chapters.summary: The clerk continues the roll call, with Council Members De La Rosa, Krishnan, Ossé, Shulman, Banks, Aldebol, and Wilson all voting aye on Intro 891-A.
chapters.title: Remaining committee members cast their votes

chapters.summary: The clerk announces the vote stands at nine in the affirmative, none in the negative, with no abstentions, and Chair Epstein thanks everyone.
chapters.title: Intro 891-A passes 9-0 with no abstentions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: The vote stands at nine in the affirmative, none in the negative, with no abstentions.

chapters.summary: When the clerk asks whether to hold the vote open, Chair Epstein says he does not think the rolls need to be kept open.
chapters.title: Epstein declines to hold the vote open

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Would you like to hold the vote open?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I don't think we need to keep the rolls open.

chapters.summary: Chair Epstein notes a member is sick and unable to attend, then adjourns the meeting, with staff and attendees exchanging thanks.
chapters.title: Epstein adjourns the meeting

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I always heard that she's sick and unable to make it today, so I'll just now adjourn this meeting.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, everyone, for being here and appreciate your time.

summary: The Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection, chaired by Harvey D. Epstein, convened a hearing to vote on Proposed Int. No. 891-A, which would prohibit surveillance pricing in New York City.

Chair Epstein delivered opening remarks tracing the history of fixed price tags from pre-1800s haggling to Macy's innovation, and explained how modern businesses use personal data to offer different prices to different consumers.
The committee held a roll call vote on Intro 891-A, which passed 9-0 with no abstentions, and the meeting was adjourned.
title: Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection
